title: Server and Client Components
summary: Decide where each component runs, draw the use client boundary in the right place, and pass data between the server and the browser safely.
intro: In a Next.js app, every component runs in one of two places: on the server, where it can read files, call APIs with secret keys, and send nothing but HTML, or in the browser, where it can hold state and respond to clicks. Choosing well makes pages fast and keeps secrets safe. Choosing badly ships a database client to every visitor, or breaks a button. This lesson explains Server Components, the "use client" line that marks the boundary, what can cross it, what the server actually sends, how to keep server code from leaking into the browser, and where context and stores fit.

steps.title: Server Components by default
steps.body:
The default decides what you get when you don't think about it. In the App Router the default is a Server Component, and knowing what that gives you and what it rules out answers most of the questions you'll have when a component won't do what you want.

## Every component starts on the server

Any component in `app/`, and any component it imports, is a **Server Component** unless its file says otherwise. Recall the idea from the React course: a Server Component runs only on the server, while the page is being made, and what it returns is sent on as HTML and RSC payload. Its code is never sent to the browser.

## What Server Components can do

Since they run on the server, they get the server's powers:

- **They can be async.** A Server Component can be an `async` function and `await` data in the middle of rendering, like the product page awaiting `getProduct(slug)`. A client component can't do that.
- **They can read what's on the server**: files on disk, a database, an internal service on your network, environment variables that hold secrets. An API key used here stays on the server, because the code that uses it never leaves.
- **They ship no JavaScript.** A big library used only in a Server Component, say one that turns Markdown into HTML, costs the browser nothing. Only its output travels.

That last point is why the default is the server. Most of a typical page, the headings, text, lists, prices, and layout, never needs to change after it arrives, so there's no reason to send the code that made it.

## What they can't do

A Server Component runs once per render, on a machine with no screen and no user, and then it's gone. So anything that needs to live on in the browser is off the table:

- **No state.** `useState` and `useReducer` keep a value between renders in the browser, and there is no "between renders" on the server.
- **No effects.** `useEffect` and `useLayoutEffect` run after the browser paints, which never happens on the server.
- **No event handlers.** An `onClick` is a function that has to run in the browser when someone clicks, so it can't come from code that never reaches the browser.
- **No browser APIs.** `window`, `document`, `localStorage`, and `navigator` don't exist on the server.

Use any of these in a Server Component, and Next.js stops with an error that says which one and how to fix it, as the example below shows. The fix is always the same idea: move the part that needs the browser into a client component, which the next part covers.

## A rule of thumb

Ask of each component: does it need state, effects, event handlers, or browser APIs? If not, leave it a Server Component. In Trailhead, the header, the product list, the product page, and the about page are all Server Components. Only a few small pieces, the quantity picker, the cart badge, and the menu links that know which page you're on, need the browser.

examples.title: A Server Component that reads a file
examples.prompt: `app/(marketing)/about/page.tsx` reads the shop's story from `content/about.txt`, a plain text file in the project.
examples.explanation: `node:fs` is Node.js's file system module, the same one any Node program uses, and it works here because this component runs on the server. `process.cwd()` is the project's folder, so the path points at `content/about.txt`. The browser receives two paragraphs of HTML and none of this code: no `fs`, no path, no file name. In the build, `/about` came out as `○`, static, since reading a file in the project gives the same text every time, so Next.js read it once, during the build. A file that changes while the app runs needs caching rules instead, which the caching lesson covers.

examples.title: State in a Server Component
examples.prompt: `app/lab/page.tsx` uses `useState` without saying it's a client component. Build the project. The output below starts where the error does.
examples.explanation: The build stops before it renders anything, and points at the import. The message names the hook, says it only works in Client Components, and gives the fix: put `"use client"` at the top of the file. The same check catches `useEffect`, `useReducer`, and the other hooks that need the browser. An `onClick` in a Server Component fails a little later, while the page is being rendered, with `Event handlers cannot be passed to Client Component props`.

steps.title: The use client boundary
steps.body:
Interactivity has to come from somewhere, and the `"use client"` line is how you say where. Where you put it decides how much JavaScript every visitor downloads, so it's the most important line you'll place in a Next.js app.

## A line at the top of a file

`"use client"` is a **directive**: a string on the first line of a file, before any imports, that tells the bundler how to treat the file. It marks the file as a client module, so its components are **Client Components**. They can use state, effects, event handlers, and browser APIs, everything you did in the React course.

It marks more than one file, though. Everything a client module imports is pulled into the browser's JavaScript too, along with what those files import, and so on down. The directive draws a **boundary**: above it, Server Components. Below it, client code. You only write `"use client"` at the entry point of each client part, not in every file under it.

```diagram server-vs-client-components-boundary
Server Components make up the tree. The client parts are small leaves, each starting at a file marked use client.
```

## Client Components still render on the server

The name misleads people. A Client Component isn't skipped on the server: during the first page load, Next.js renders it there too, into HTML, so the visitor sees the quantity picker straight away instead of a hole. Then its JavaScript is downloaded, and React hydrates it, attaching the handlers so the buttons work. "Client" means it also runs in the browser, not that it runs only there.

That has a practical consequence you met in the React course: the first render of a Client Component must give the same result on the server and in the browser, or hydration complains. Don't read `window`, `localStorage`, or the current time while rendering. Read them in an effect, or with `useSyncExternalStore`, after hydration.

## Push the boundary to the leaves

Since everything below the line ships to the browser, put the line as low in the tree as you can. Suppose a product page needs one interactive piece, a quantity picker. You could mark the whole page `"use client"`. It would work, but now the page, its text, its formatting helpers, and every component it uses ship to the browser, and the page can't be async or read data on the server anymore.

Instead, make the quantity picker its own small client component, and leave the page a Server Component that renders it. The page's text arrives as HTML, and only the picker's few lines of code are downloaded. Look at the diagram: the client parts are three leaves, and everything above them stays on the server.

## How the two kinds fit together

Two rules follow from where each kind runs:

- **A Server Component can render a Client Component** and pass it props, like `<QuantityPicker max={10} />`. That's the normal case.
- **A Client Component can't import a Server Component.** Importing it into a client file would pull it into the browser bundle, where it can't run. It can, however, render one that it receives as a prop, which the next part shows.

When you need hooks, use the ones from the React course as before: `useState` and `useReducer` for state, `useEffect` to sync with something outside React, refs for the DOM. Nothing about them changes inside a Client Component.

examples.title: A small client component
examples.prompt: `components/quantity-picker.tsx` holds the only state on the product page: how many to add.
examples.explanation: `"use client"` comes first, before the imports. The component keeps the quantity in state, between 1 and `max`, and the updater functions you met in the React course keep it from going out of range. `output` with `aria-live` makes screen readers announce the new number. `useCartStore` reads the cart's `add` action from a Zustand store, which the last part of this lesson sets up. For now it only counts items in the browser, and the Server Actions lesson later sends them to the API. On the first load, this renders on the server as HTML showing 1, then hydrates, and the buttons start working.

examples.title: The Server Component page that uses it
examples.prompt: `app/products/[slug]/page.tsx` stays a Server Component and renders the picker as a leaf.
examples.explanation: The page has no `"use client"`, so it stays async and fetches its own data. It decides on the server whether to show the picker at all: an out-of-stock product gets plain text and downloads no picker code. For one in stock, it passes `max`, the smaller of the stock and 10, since the API allows at most 10 of an item in the cart. `formatPrice` and `getProduct` run here and are never sent to the browser. Only `QuantityPicker` and what it imports cross the boundary.

steps.title: Passing data across the boundary
steps.body:
Props are how a Server Component hands data to a Client Component, but those props have to travel from one computer to another, as text. Not every JavaScript value survives that trip, and knowing which ones do saves you from errors that only appear when the page renders.

## Props must be serializable

To **serialize** a value is to turn it into text that can be sent and turned back into the same value on the other side, the way `JSON.stringify` does. Props going from a Server Component to a Client Component are serialized into the RSC payload, so they must be values React knows how to serialize:

- Strings, numbers, booleans, `null`, and `undefined`, plus `bigint`.
- Plain objects and arrays made of those.
- `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, and typed arrays.
- JSX: elements, including Server Components already rendered.
- Promises of any of those.
- Server Functions, the functions marked `"use server"` that the Server Actions lesson covers.

What doesn't cross: ordinary functions, class instances with methods, and symbols you made yourself. A function can't be sent, since its code would have to run on the other side, and it may close over server variables that must never leave. Pass data, not behavior: the price in cents instead of a formatting function, and let the client component format it, or format it on the server and pass the text.

## Server Components as children

A Client Component can't import a Server Component, but it can receive one already rendered, as `children` or any other prop. The Server Component renders on the server, and the client component gets its output as JSX, the same way it would get a string. So a client wrapper, like a section that opens and closes, can hold server-rendered content inside it without that content becoming client code. This is the children and composition pattern from the React course, and in Next.js it's how you keep the boundary at the leaves even when an interactive part wraps a big piece of the page.

## Promises, read with use

A Server Component can start a request and hand the unfinished promise to a Client Component, without waiting for it. The Client Component reads it with React's `use`, which you met in the React course: inside a `Suspense` boundary, `use(promise)` shows the fallback until the promise settles, then renders with its value. The server keeps working in the meantime and streams the value down when it's ready. It's a way to start slow data early on the server and still show it in a client component, and the data lessons come back to it.

## Functions, the one exception

The only functions allowed across the boundary are **Server Functions**, async functions in a file or function marked `"use server"`. They don't actually travel: the client gets a reference, and calling it sends a request to the server, which runs the real function. That's how forms and buttons will change data later in the course.

examples.title: A function as a prop
examples.prompt: `app/lab/page.tsx` passes `formatPrice` to `PriceTag`, a client component in `app/lab/price-tag.tsx` that calls it. Build the project. The output below starts where the error does.
examples.explanation: The build fails while rendering the page. The message says functions can't be passed to Client Components, and it points at the exact prop: `cents: 34900` was fine, `format: function` wasn't. Its other suggestion, that you meant to call the function, is the usual fix: pass `formatPrice(34900)`, the text, or import `formatPrice` inside the client component, where it then ships as client code. An event handler gets its own wording, `Event handlers cannot be passed to Client Component props`, for the same reason.

examples.title: Server content inside a client wrapper
examples.prompt: `components/collapsible.tsx` is a client component that shows or hides whatever it's given as `children`.
examples.explanation:
The product page uses it as `

{product.description}

`. The paragraph is made by the Server Component, so the description is rendered on the server and arrives in the payload as finished JSX. `Collapsible` only decides whether to show it. Its own code is a few lines, and it never needs to know where its children came from, so the same wrapper could hold a whole server-rendered table. `aria-expanded` tells screen readers whether the section is open.

examples.title: A promise read with use
examples.prompt:
The product page runs `const reviews = getReviews(slug);` with no `await`, then renders `` inside `Loading reviews…

}>`. This is `components/review-list.tsx`.
examples.explanation: Since the page doesn't wait for `getReviews`, it carries on while the request is out. The reviews take about a second to arrive, so the server sends everything else first, with Loading reviews… in their place. When the promise settles, the server streams the reviews down, and `use` hands them to the list. On the Ridge 2P Tent page the list read 5/5 Two doors make all the difference, by Lee, then 4/5 Dry through a storm, by Priya. The Camp Kettle has no reviews, so its page shows No reviews yet. If the promise rejects, the nearest `error.tsx` shows instead. The promise is a prop like any other: React serializes it, and the value follows when it's ready. `import type` brings in only the `Review` type, which the build erases, so none of the server code in `lib/products.ts` comes along.

steps.title: What the server sends: the RSC payload
steps.body:
When something goes wrong between the server and the browser, or a page downloads more than it should, the RSC payload is where the answer is. You don't need to read it every day, but being able to read it once makes the whole model concrete.

## What's in it

The RSC payload is the rendered tree of a page, written as lines of text. Each line has an id, a colon, and a value. Server Components don't appear in it at all, only what they returned: plain elements like `article` and `h1`, with their props and text, already worked out. Where a Client Component sits in the tree, the payload has a **client reference** instead: a pointer that says which component it is, which JavaScript files hold it, and what props it gets.

```diagram server-vs-client-components-payload
The server sends what its components returned. A client component is a reference to the chunk that holds its code.
```

In step 1, the product page runs on the server, with `getProduct` and `formatPrice`. In step 2, its output becomes payload lines: the `article` element and its children, with the price already formatted, and a row that starts with `I`, which names `QuantityPicker` and its chunks. In step 3, React in the browser draws the plain elements as they are. For the reference, it loads the chunk, a small JavaScript file the bundler made, and runs `QuantityPicker` with the props from the payload.

## HTML first, payload on navigation

On a first visit, the server sends HTML so the page shows before any JavaScript, and the payload rides along inside the HTML in `script` tags, so React can hydrate without asking again. On a later soft navigation, the router asks only for the payload, as the lesson that created the project showed, since the browser already has React and can build the new page from it.

## Seeing it in the Network panel

Build and start the app, open DevTools, and pick the Network tab. Click from the product list to a product. Among the new rows is one named like `ember-stove?_rsc=…` with the type `text/x-component`. Open it and choose Response to read the payload, the same lines the example below shows. Rows with `_rsc` in their names that appear before you click are prefetches, and they're mostly the App Shell: layouts and loading states.

## Why moving work to the server shrinks the bundle

Look at what's missing from the payload: `getProduct`, the API's address, the fetch, `formatPrice`, the `Intl.NumberFormat` it uses, and the page component itself. All of that ran on the server and stayed there. The browser got the results, `$64.00`, as text. In a single-page app, all of that code would have been in the bundle, downloaded and run by every visitor before the price appeared. In the App Router, the only JavaScript a page sends is React, the router, and the client components it actually uses. Each component you keep on the server, and each library only it uses, is code no visitor has to download.

examples.title: A product's payload
examples.prompt: The Response tab of the `_rsc` request for the Ember Stove page, trimmed to the lines about the product. Each line is shown exactly as it arrived.
examples.code:
18:"/_next/static/chunks/1yqjf9cm5y4xk.js"
19:"/_next/static/chunks/1xpfcun70amb_.js"
1a:I[24757,["$7","$18","$19"],"QuantityPicker"]
6:["$","article",null,{"children":[["$","h1",null,{"className":"text-2xl font-semibold","children":"Ember Stove"}],["$","p",null,{"children":"$$64.00"}],["$","p",null,{"children":"A compact canister stove that boils a liter of water in about four minutes."}],["$","$L1a",null,{"max":10}]]}]
examples.explanation: Lines `18` and `19` are paths to JavaScript chunks. Line `1a` is the client reference: `I` for import, `24757` is the module's id in the bundle, the list says which chunks to load, with `$18` meaning the value on line `18`, and `"QuantityPicker"` is the export to use. Line `6` is the product page's output. Each element is written as `["$", type, key, props]`, so `["$","h1",null,{…"children":"Ember Stove"}]` is the heading. The price is `$$64.00`, because a string that starts with `$` gets a second `$` to show it isn't a reference. The last child, `["$","$L1a",null,{"max":10}]`, is the picker: its type is `$L1a`, the reference on line `1a`, and its props are `{"max":10}`. The page component, the fetch, and the formatting code appear nowhere.

steps.title: Keeping server code on the server
steps.body:
A mistake on the boundary can do worse than break a button. Import the wrong module into a client component, and the code inside it, the API's internal address, the query that reads your database, ships to every visitor. Next.js has two safety nets for this, and both only work if you use them.

## server-only and client-only

`server-only` is a tiny npm package with one job: importing it from code that ends up in the browser makes the build fail. Put `import "server-only";` at the top of any module that must never reach the browser, like the one that calls the API with a secret key or talks to the database, and a mistaken import from a client component becomes a build error instead of a leak. Install it with `npm install server-only`.

`client-only` is the mirror image, for code that only makes sense in the browser, like a module that reads `window` as soon as it loads. Importing it from a Server Component fails the build.

## Server environment variables are empty in the browser

Recall from the lesson that created the project that only variables named `NEXT_PUBLIC_` reach the browser. Next.js copies their values into the client JavaScript during the build, and leaves every other `process.env` value out. So a client component that reads `process.env.API_URL` gets `undefined` in the browser. That protects your secrets, but it also means code that silently does the wrong thing, like fetching from `undefined/products`, instead of failing loudly. It's one more reason to keep API calls in server-only modules.

Never fix it by renaming a secret to `NEXT_PUBLIC_`. The name is the decision to publish the value, and anyone can read it in the JavaScript your site sends.

## A server-only data module

Put the two ideas together, and you get the shape most Next.js apps use: one module, or a small folder of them, that does all the talking to the API or the database, and starts with `import "server-only"`. In Trailhead it's `lib/api.ts`, with `apiFetch`, and `lib/products.ts`, with `listProducts`, `getProduct`, and `getReviews`, built on it. Pages and Server Components import from there. Client components never do: when they need data, a Server Component fetches it and passes it down as props, or passes a promise. The security lesson builds this into a full data access layer that also checks who's asking.

examples.title: A module that refuses the browser
examples.prompt: `lib/api.ts`, the one place Trailhead calls the API from. Its first line is the guard.
examples.explanation: `apiFetch` adds the API's base address from `API_URL`, set in `.env`, and turns any status that isn't 2xx into an `ApiError` that carries the status. A client component that imported `getProduct` from `lib/products.ts`, which imports this file, failed the build with two errors. The clearer one read `'server-only' cannot be imported from a Client Component module` and `It should only be used from a Server Component`, followed by the chain of imports that led there, ending at the client file. The other wording in the same output talks about the Pages Router, which is misleading here: the import trace is the part to read.

examples.title: process.env in a client component
examples.prompt: A client component with a button that logs two variables, one public and one not. The build ran with `NEXT_PUBLIC_SHOP_NAME=Trailhead` set. Click the button and read the browser's console.
examples.explanation: `API_URL` is `undefined` in the browser, although the server has it, because it isn't public. `NEXT_PUBLIC_SHOP_NAME` shows its value, and a search of the built JavaScript in `.next/static/chunks` found the text `Trailhead` written into one of the chunks. That's what being inlined at build time means: the value is baked into the file, so changing it later means building again. This button reads the variables in a click handler on purpose. Rendering `process.env.API_URL` directly would show the value in the server's HTML and nothing in the browser's, and hydration would complain about the mismatch.

steps.title: Context, stores, and third-party components
steps.body:
Context providers, stores, and most npm UI libraries were written for apps that run entirely in the browser. They all work in Next.js, but each one needs a client component somewhere, and putting it in the right place keeps the rest of the app on the server.

## Providers in a client wrapper

Recall context from the React course: a provider component makes a value available to everything below it. A provider uses state and context, so it has to be a Client Component, and a Server Component, like the root layout, can't create a context itself. The pattern is a small client file that holds the provider, which the layout renders around `children`.

That doesn't turn the app into client code. `children` is passed in already rendered, as the last part showed, so the pages inside the provider stay Server Components. Only the provider's own code, and the components that read the context, run in the browser. Put the provider as deep as it can go: a theme might need the whole app, while a provider used only on account pages belongs in the account layout.

## A Zustand store per request

The React course created a Zustand store at the top of a module with `create()`, one store for the whole app. In a single-page app that's fine: one browser, one visitor. On a server, a module is loaded once and shared by every request it handles. A store at the top of a module would be shared by every visitor's server render, so one person's cart could appear in another person's HTML.

So in Next.js, create the store inside a provider instead, once per render, and share it through context. Each request renders its own provider and gets its own store, and in the browser the provider creates it once and keeps it. Zustand's `createStore` makes a store without binding it to React, and its `useStore` hook reads one passed in, which is exactly the shape this needs. The example builds Trailhead's cart store this way.

## TanStack Query, if you want it

If parts of your app fetch in the browser with TanStack Query, from the React course, its `QueryClientProvider` goes in a client wrapper too, with the `QueryClient` created inside it in the same once-per-render way. A Server Component can even fetch the first data with `queryClient.prefetchQuery` and hand it over with TanStack Query's `HydrationBoundary`, so the client starts with a full cache. Most Next.js pages don't need it, since Server Components fetch on the server already. The data lessons explain when browser fetching is still the right choice.

## Third-party components

Many UI libraries ship components that use state or effects but don't start with `"use client"`, because they were written before Server Components existed. Use one directly in a Server Component, and you get the same hooks error as before. The fix is a one-line wrapper: a file with `"use client"` that imports the component and exports it again, like `export { Carousel } from "some-carousel";` under the directive. Server Components then import your wrapper. Libraries that support Server Components already include the directive, and need no wrapper.

examples.title: A cart store, one per request
examples.prompt: `stores/cart-store.tsx` holds the store, the provider that creates it, and a hook to read it.
examples.explanation: `createCartStore` makes a new store each time it's called. The provider calls it once, in `useState`'s initializer, so each render on the server gets a fresh store, while in the browser the same store lives as long as the provider does. `<CartStoreContext value={store}>` is React 19's way of rendering a provider, from the React course, and `use(CartStoreContext)` reads it. `useCartStore` takes a selector, like Zustand's own hook, so a component re-renders only when the part it reads changes. With Zustand 5.1, adding 3 Ember Stoves on a product page made the header's badge read Cart (3), and it still did after a click to the product list, since the provider lives in the root layout.

examples.title: The root layout with the provider
examples.prompt: `app/layout.tsx` wraps the header and every page in the cart provider.
examples.explanation: The layout stays a Server Component: it imports a client component and renders it, which is allowed. `SiteHeader` and every page are passed in as children, already rendered on the server, so they stay Server Components inside a client provider. Only the components that call `useCartStore`, the `CartBadge` in the header and the `QuantityPicker`, read the store. `initialCount` is 0 for now. Loading the real count means reading the visitor's cookie, which the data lessons show how to do without making the whole layout wait.

recap:
- Components in app/ are Server Components by default: they can be async, read files and secrets, and ship no JavaScript.
- Server Components can't use state, effects, event handlers, or browser APIs.
- "use client" at the top of a file marks it and everything it imports as client code, so put it on small leaves.
- Client Components still render to HTML on the server first, then hydrate in the browser.
- Props that cross the boundary must be serializable. Pass data and rendered JSX, and promises read with use.
- The RSC payload holds rendered elements and references to client chunks. Server code never appears in it.
- import "server-only" turns a leak into a build error, and non-public env variables are undefined in the browser.
- Providers and stores go in client wrappers, with a Zustand store created per request, never at module level.
